[00:07:40] I think I'm going to go top left to bottom right.

[00:07:45] And there's been a lot of different tricks
[00:07:47] and a lot of things that people have done in the open source

[00:08:01] I think, really, the oldest and in some ways
[00:08:04] the most visionary of this is things like FLAN.

[00:08:14] NLP people have already collected
[00:08:16] a bunch of supervised data sets of inputs and outputs.

[00:08:22] Reasonable thing to try.
[00:08:25] Turned out, for various reasons, this
[00:08:26] was not the right thing to do.
[00:08:27] I'll talk about that later.
[00:08:29] Self-instruct, and other follow ups to that, this was also
[00:08:33] very forward-looking in terms of its thinking was saying, well,
[00:08:36] why can't we use the model itself to generate data?
[00:08:39] Well, models are getting better all the time.
[00:08:41] And in fact, they might even be better than some
[00:08:43] of our annotators.
[00:08:45] Why don't we get models to write very good, high quality
[00:08:50] responses to our inputs?
[00:08:51] And that's the self-construct idea.
[00:08:53] And then there came a bunch of distillation style approaches.
[00:08:57] Alpaca is one of them.
[00:08:59] The Berkeley folks had one called
[00:09:00] Vicuna in which they were using online user shared
[00:09:05] prompts as the way to-- as the inputs to distill on.
[00:09:09] And then there were other efforts
[00:09:11] that were more entirely human-driven,
[00:09:13] like Open Assistant.
[00:09:14] You can think of this kind of like Wikipedia.
[00:09:16] It was a bunch of people getting together
[00:09:18] to write prompts and responses.
[00:09:20] And then you have a new generation WizardLM
[00:09:23] and Tulu3 and others of saying, well,
[00:09:26] that language models are very good synthetic data generators.
[00:09:29] Why don't we come up with increasingly complicated ways
[00:09:32] of generating instruction following
[00:09:34] data using language models?
[00:09:36] And then finally, I'll touch briefly on this.
[00:09:39] SFT and post-training has changed yet again
[00:09:42] in recent years because I think the focus is less on chat,
[00:09:45] and much more on agents and tool use.
[00:09:47] And so there is now a new generation of SFT pipelines
[00:09:51] that are designed to generate tool use and agentic data.
[00:09:54] So this is roughly a bunch of different developments
[00:09:58] in post-training data land, at least in the open source world.

[01:14:55] they did DPO.
[01:14:57] And then they used that DPO model
[01:14:59] to then generate candidates that the rejection sampled and they
[01:15:02] repeated this process.
[01:15:03] So there's the outer loop on top of it.
[01:15:04] But basically, the core RLHF primitive for Llama was DPO.
[01:15:10] In the years since, there's been a lot
[01:15:12] of different variants of DPO.
[01:15:15] There was SimPO, which basically changes the weighting.
[01:15:18] So instead of using pi ref, you have this y of l normalizer.
[01:15:24] There was length normalized DPO, which normalizes by the length
[01:15:28] in order to avoid certain length hacking
[01:15:30] issues that seem to arise.
[01:15:33] But really, none of these variants
[01:15:36] maybe seem to matter very much.
[01:15:39] One of the things that I'll mention,
[01:15:40] that I thought was very interesting,
[01:15:42] was these results are very, very contingent on the specifics
[01:15:45] of the experiment setup.
[01:15:47] So even at Ai2, there was a paper that was like, well,
[01:15:51] it turns out that if you go from DPO to PPO,
[01:15:54] you'll get a better result. But then they also
[01:15:58] had a paper for Tulu2, where they said, actually,
[01:16:01] if you do DPO right, you can do better than PPO.
[01:16:05] And so depending on how you execute this,
[01:16:09] one can be better than the other.
[01:16:10] I'm sure you have experiences reading deep learning
[01:16:12] papers and so on, where the results are very fragile.
[01:16:16] So maybe the takeaway from all of this
[01:16:18] is that these DPO variants are actually
[01:16:20] close enough to the right thing to give you pretty
[01:16:22] good performance in many cases.
[01:16:24] This core idea of take gradient step in the right direction
[01:16:27] and take negative gradient step from the bad stuff
[01:16:30] works reasonably well as long as you set the step sizes right.
[01:16:34] OK.
[01:16:35] I will end with the last few slides on things
[01:16:37] to watch out for in RLHF.
[01:16:40] So one of the things to watch out for is over optimization.
[01:16:43] And this is maybe one of the biggest things.
[01:16:46] To give you also historical context,
[01:16:48] when InstructGPT came out, and people were very excited
[01:16:52] about this, I think there was a very real question
[01:16:54] can we RLHF our way to superintelligent systems
[01:16:58] or whatever?
[01:16:59] Maybe we can.
[01:16:59] Just collect enough thumbs up, thumbs down.
[01:17:01] Turns out that is actually quite challenging.
[01:17:04] Because you find that if you try to really push the RLHF
[01:17:08] process forward, you'll start overfitting
[01:17:11] to your learned reward model.
[01:17:13] So the KL regularizer that I talked about
[01:17:15] is really critical in a lot of cases in order
[01:17:18] to prevent your optimization process
[01:17:21] from overfitting your reward model,
[01:17:24] at least if your optimization process is very good.
[01:17:27] The other thing that I'll talk about is model collapse.
[01:17:32] So people have seen lots of times, where RL models have
[01:17:36] much less diversity.
[01:17:37] They're concentrated on a few different possible outputs.
[01:17:40] And this connects back to what I said before right RLHF
[01:17:43] models are really no longer modeling
[01:17:46] a distribution which comes with its own inherent diversity.
[01:17:49] It's a policy that can collapse as
[01:17:51] long as it gets a good reward.
[01:17:52] So this is another thing that RLHF models have really
[01:17:56] struggled with in recent years.
[01:18:01] So actually, I'm going to skip this because we're at time.
[01:18:04] And I think this entropy and mode collapse thing actually
[01:18:07] ends up being quite important even today.
[01:18:11] And the GPT-4 era actually was one of the few plots
[01:18:14] that OpenAI put out, where they said, actually, we
[01:18:16] have a few open problems left.
[01:18:17] And one of the open problems they had was,
[01:18:19] actually, our models are uncalibrated
[01:18:21] after we do RLHF, which you can see in this plot over here.
[01:18:24] I don't think anyone has really solved that yet.
[01:18:27] The Anthropic folks also had an argument saying, well,
[01:18:31] it's naturally uncalibrated.
[01:18:32] You could recalibrate sometimes, but not always.
[01:18:35] This becomes very important in the next lecture
[01:18:38] when we talk about things like RLVR,
[01:18:40] where the entropy and exploration is actually
[01:18:42] quite critical for the model to explore
[01:18:45] all the possible solutions, and to make progress on some
[01:18:47] of these very hard problems.
[01:18:50] Great.
[01:18:52] So to put it all together, RLHF data collection
[01:18:56] is also very hard.
[01:18:57] I think part of the thing about post-training
[01:18:59] is it's very complicated, messy process because a lot of it
[01:19:02] is getting good data.
[01:19:04] And getting good data is always very difficult.
[01:19:07] RLHF algorithms are quite complex.
[01:19:09] PPO is especially difficult. I'll talk a little bit about it
[01:19:12] next lecture.
[01:19:13] Thankfully, we do also have a simpler variant.
[01:19:16] They're called GRPO.
[01:19:16] That works pretty well.
[01:19:17] That's what you'll do in your assignments.
[01:19:19] But this is one place where there's been
[01:19:21] a lot of recent developments.
[01:19:23] Finally, I think, in terms of RLHF,
[01:19:25] one of the big, big problems is over optimization.
[01:19:29] And the transition to the next lecture
[01:19:30] is going to be, is there rewards where we won't over optimize
[01:19:34] or we can just dumping compute and the model performance just
[01:19:37] keeps monotonically getting better.
[01:19:39] And that's one of the reasons why what people call
[01:19:41] RLVR is just so been so impactful.
[01:19:45] Thanks.
